1.2.2.6-f14.accuracy_reason: Gellius 19.10 quotes Ennius (Iphigenia) as 'otio qui nescit uti plus negoti habet quam cum est negotium in negotio'. Burton does drop 'cum est', though he also adds 'qui' and changes the word order.

1.2.2.6-f18.accuracy_reason: Gellius 19.10 gives Ennius' line as 'incerte errat animus, praeter propter vitam vivitur', and 'praeter propter' does mean roughly 'at random'. 'vitiam' is clearly a corruption of 'vitam'.

1.2.2.6-f29.accuracy_reason: Aeneid 4.73 ('haeret lateri letalis harundo') ends the simile of Dido as a wounded deer.

1.2.2.6-f38.accuracy_reason: Aristotle, Politics 1.2 (1253a) says a man outside the city is either a beast or a god. Burton's own English does render 'Deus' as 'a Saint'.

1.2.2.6-f40.accuracy_reason: The Vulgate at Ecclesiastes 4:10 reads 'vae soli, quia cum ruerit, non habet sublevantem', not 'cum ceciderit'. 'Ceciderit' belongs to the clause just before it.

1.2.2.6-f41.accuracy_reason: Hosea 13:9: the KJV reads 'O Israel, thou hast destroyed thyself', the Vulgate 'Perditio tua, Israel; tantummodo in me auxilium tuum'. 'Perditio tua ex te' is the traditional proverbial form.

1.2.2.6-f45.accuracy_reason: It is rightly hedged: Diego de Estella's 'De contemnendis mundi vanitatibus' (Vanity of the World) fits a list of writers who praise withdrawal from the world.

1.2.2.6-f46.accuracy_reason: Cassius Dio 69.19 tells of Similis, Hadrian's praetorian prefect, who retired and had it written on his tomb that he had lived only seven years.

1.2.2.6-f62.accuracy_reason: Seneca, Ep. 55.3 does read 'O Vatia, solus scis vivere'. But calling Burton's 'Vatia lives alone' a misreading is stated too surely: he may have bent the phrase on purpose to fit his theme of solitude.

1.2.2.6-f63.accuracy_reason: Cicero, De Officiis 3.1 does give Scipio's saying in indirect speech, with the 'otiosum' clause first.
